extraction.name: ChartQA
extraction.description: A large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts with visual and logical reasoning, covering 9.6K human-written questions and 23.1K machine-generated questions from human-written chart summaries across 20,882 charts from four different online sources.
extraction.creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
extraction.citeAs: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque. ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning. arXiv:2203.10244v1 [cs.CL] 19 Mar 2022
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Charts were crawled from four different sources: (i) Statista (statista.com) - an online platform presenting charts covering various topics including economy, politics, and industry; (ii) The Pew research (pewresearch.org) - publishes reports about social and economic issues, demographic trends and public opinion; (iii) Our World In Data or OWID (ourworldindata.org) - contains thousands of charts about global issues such as economy, finance, and society; (iv) Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development or OECD (oecd.org) - shares reports and data analysis for policymaking. For Pew dataset, only chart images were crawled. For the other three, underlying data tables, metadata (e.g., title, chart type), SVG file and associate text description were extracted. Bounding boxes information of different chart elements (e.g., x-axis labels) were extracted from SVG files.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Charts and associated data were collected from four online sources: Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data (OWID), and OECD. These sources provide publicly available charts covering various topics including economy, politics, industry, social issues, demographic trends, and public opinion.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For the Pew dataset, only chart images were crawled since the underlying data tables are not available. For the other three sources (Statista, OWID, OECD), the underlying data tables, metadata (e.g., title, chart type), SVG file and associate text description were extracted. Bounding boxes information of the different chart elements (e.g., x-axis labels) were extracted from the SVG files to train data extraction models.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The ChartOCR model was adapted to extract the underlying data table from chart images. The process involves three main stages: (1) key-point detection networks locate chart visual marks (e.g. bars, plot area, line points) and textual elements (e.g. x-axis-label, legend-label); (2) chart scale is estimated using y-axis-labels value for line and bar charts, and for pie charts the value of each segment is estimated by calculating the angle between its borderlines; (3) the model aggregates extracted data values using color and proximity heuristics to output the final raw data values and fully-structured data table with textual labels. The CRAFT model was utilized to recognize texts in chart elements. Data values were associated with text labels using positional and color information.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Two main annotation procedures were used: (i) Human-authored QA pairs collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) where crowdworkers were asked to focus on two types of questions for each chart image: compositional questions (containing at least two mathematical/logical operations like sum, difference and average) and visual questions (referring to visual attributes such as color, height, and length of graphical marks). For each chart, workers provided two questions with answers. The same questions were then answered by another annotator. If both workers' answers exactly matched, the answer was considered correct. Otherwise, answers were manually checked to select the final correct answer. Overall agreement between crowd workers based on exact matches was 61.04%, but manual checking on 500 random samples found agreement to be 78.55% when considering typos and lexical variations. (ii) Machine-generated QA pairs from Statista human-written summaries using a T5 model fine-tuned on the SQuAD QA dataset. The process involved training two T5 models: one for answer extraction and another for answer-aware question generation. A heuristic was developed to filter out invalid questions by checking if the answer could be found in the chart data table. Manual analysis of 1,250 QA pairs found that 86.64% were complete, answerable, and correct. The test set of the machine generated dataset was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For human-authored questions, if both workers' answers exactly matched, the answer was considered correct. Otherwise, answers were manually checked to select the final correct answer. Overall agreement between crowd workers based on exact matches was 61.04%. However, manual checking on 500 random samples found agreement to be much higher (78.55%) when considering typos and lexical variations (e.g., 3$ vs. 3 dollars, 86.33 vs 86.3). For machine-generated questions, after applying filtering heuristics, manual analysis of 1,250 QA pairs found that 86.64% were complete, answerable, and correct given the chart.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: For human-authored questions: each chart received two questions with answers from one worker, and the same questions were answered by another annotator (2 annotations per question).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Workers were selected with an acceptance rate of 95% and total accomplished HITs of 5000. Workers were further filtered by giving them a pre-test to select the best qualified workers for the task. Annotators were fairly compensated considering the minimum wage in the United States at the time ($7.25 USD per hour), receiving $0.6 USD for each task estimated to take 3-5 minutes.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 model (fine-tuned on SQuAD QA dataset) for automatic question generation from human-written chart summaries. ChartOCR model (adapted from Luo et al., 2021) for automatic chart data extraction. CRAFT model (Baek et al., 2019) for text recognition in chart elements. Mask R-CNN (He et al., 2017) with Resnet-101 backbone for extracting visual features of chart marks.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The models can be abused to mislead the public about the charts content and implications. While the models provide state-of-the-art results on most of the existing datasets, there is no guarantee that their output will be correct all the time. Current approaches for automatic data extraction are modular and combine deep learning and rule-based methods which are error-prone. The accuracy of data extraction is specifically lower on line and dot line charts in FigureQA and PlotQA. In DVQA, extracted tables from logarithmic-scale charts were quite noisy since ChartOCR does not support them. PlotQA has many charts with very large values (usually written in E notation), and errors in such figures have higher impact on overall accuracy. The accuracy on PlotQA and ChartQA are generally lower since they have more complex charts. A major limitation of evaluation metrics for chart data extraction is that they do not take the extracted textual tokens into consideration (which are much more noisy in real-world figures). Models cannot effectively handle nested operations. Complex visual compositional questions may require a multi-stage reasoning process that current input representations do not fully capture.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training and evaluating Chart Question Answering (ChartQA) systems that help users by taking a chart and a natural language question as input and predicting the answer. The benchmark focuses on visual and logical reasoning questions about charts. The dataset was split into train, validation, and test sets for model development and evaluation. ChartQA-H (human-written): Training (3,699 charts, 7,398 questions), Validation (480 charts, 960 questions), Test (625 charts, 1,250 questions). ChartQA-M (machine-generated): Training (15,474 charts, 20,901 questions), Validation (680 charts, 960 questions), Test (987 charts, 1,250 questions).
